newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Transition to Euro notes too long - Belgian c.banker.
newsitem.headline: Transition to Euro notes too long - Belgian c.banker.

text.p: Belgian National Bank Governor Alfons Verplaetse said on Thursday the planned six-month transitional period to introduce euro notes and coins was too long.
"I'm convinced the maximum period of six months in which (there are both) European and national bank notes is too much," Verplaetse told a Flanders Technology Foundation lunch meeting.
He noted that East German marks were changed into West German marks in one night after Germany's reunification. "But of course, they are Germans," he quipped.

Under the planned Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) transition scenario, the euro will be introduced in 1999 for banks, financial markets and governments. But national currencies will remain in circulation until at the latest January 1, 2002, after which there will be a six-month period during which they are gradually replaced by euros.
Verplaetse dismissed suggestions by European Monetary Institute head Alexandre Lamfalussy in a recent newspaper interview that European Union national currencies could disappear earlier than 2002.
"It will be very hard to introduce the euro before let's say November 15, 2001," Verplaetse said.
"If you see all the tasks that have to be carried out, all the pension payments...refunding...all in the euro, I don't think that period can be reduced much," he said.
He added it would be ridiculous to introduce the euro on December 31, ahead of end-of-year festivities.
Verplaetse said Britain would probably delay signing up to the European Union's planned single currency.
EMU is due to be launched on January 1, 1999, but the British government has yet to decide whether it will take part.
"I don't believe at all that the British will want to join (EMU) on January 1, 1999," he said.
But he added he believed Britain would eventully join and that Europe needed Britain, "but more politically."
"Sooner than we think the British, who can calculate well, who are super diplomats, will join EMU," he said.

"That's why I say 'wait for the right time but please let us get on, without you (the British)'," said Verplaetse, who added that EMU was a stepping stone to political integration and not a goal in itself.
"Monetary union is a very important step, a challenge without precedent, but - and it may surprise you to hear this from a (central bank) governor - it's not a goal as such," he said.
Verplaetse said EMU would herald greater European integration, gradually including all forms of taxation.
"Eventually we'll arrive at political integraton, which is the main goal of the whole monetary union," he said.
